state.misconception_label: Confuses rest and movement on a distance time graph

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: This graph shows how far Fido the dog is from his home. What might the negative-sloping section represent? ![A graph with time (secs) on the horizontal axis and distance (m) on the vertical axis. The graph starts at the origin, travels in a straight line up and right, travels horizontally, then travels in a straight line down and right back to the x-axis. ](). I got Fido has fallen asleep because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: The negative-sloping section on a distance-time graph represents movement away from the starting point. In this case, it shows that Fido is moving further away from his home. Make sure to focus on the direction of the line to determine rest versus movement.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh, okay! So the negative slope means Fido is actually moving away from home, not falling asleep. But what does it mean when the line is flat? Does that mean he's just standing still?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Yes, exactly! A flat line on a distance-time graph indicates that Fido is at rest and not moving at all. Remember, the slope of the line represents the speed or rate of movement. So a flat line means no change in distance over time, which means Fido is stationary.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher provides mathematically incorrect information (claiming negative slope means moving away when it actually means returning home), fails to engage with the student's specific misconception about rest vs. movement, simply tells answers without prompting reasoning, and the student's final statement shows they haven't corrected their original confusion about what the flat section represents.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently states explicit rules about graph interpretation (negative slope means movement, flat line means rest), provides direct corrective feedback on the student's misconception, and clearly explains the procedural relationship between slope and movement throughout both turns.
